title: Trends and outcomes in diabetic ketoacidosis: A 10-year retrospective study at a Norwegian university hospital
content:
by Sebastian Breivik Soleim, Kristian Løvås, Eirik Søfteland, Grethe Åstrøm Ueland

Aims

To describe trends in diabetic ketoacidosis admissions and examine factors associated with repeated admissions and mortality among adults living with type 1 diabetes.

Materials and methods

Diabetic ketoacidosis admissions among adults at a Norwegian university hospital between 1 August 2012 and 31 August 2022 were retrospectively reviewed using electronic medical records.

Results

A total of 178 participants with 306 admissions were included. Median [IQR] age at admission was 34 years [22–51]. Median HbA1c was 88 mmol/mol [72–105]. Diabetic ketoacidosis admission frequency decreased by an estimated 6.9% annually (RR 0.931; 95% CI 0.896–0.968; p < 0.001) over the 10-year period. 40 participants (22.5%) had more than one admission during the study period. Psychiatric illness (aOR 2.827; 95% CI 1.070–7.468; p = 0.036) and receipt of disability benefits (aOR 4.941; 95% CI 1.576–15.490; p = 0.006) were associated with experiencing more than one lifetime admission. Prior diabetic ketoacidosis, suspected treatment non-adherence and psychiatric illness were associated with higher readmission rates during follow-up. In-hospital mortality was 1.6%, and 5-year cumulative mortality was 14.7%. Alcohol or substance misuse (HR 2.499; 95% CI: 1.191–5.245; p = 0.015) and higher age at the index admission (HR 1.874; 95% CI: 1.511–2.324; p < 0.001, per 10 years) were associated with mortality in the follow-up period.

Conclusions

Diabetic ketoacidosis admissions declined substantially over the 10-year study period despite growth in the hospital catchment area population, suggesting that diabetes care has improved. Repeated admissions were common and associated with psychosocial vulnerability. In-hospital mortality was low, but five-year mortality was considerable, supporting targeted follow-up after an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis.
